commitResults.messageBody:
Project-specific Claude Code skill based on se-edu/skill-present-changes-visually,
generating a self-contained GitHub-style split-view HTML diff of repo changes.
Adapted paths (.claude/skills instead of .codex/skills) and the interpreter
invocation (py launcher) for this environment.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add test-ui skill and console UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
Project-specific Claude Code skill that drives the compiled program one
command at a time against test/ui-test-plan.md, comparing each response to
its expected output and stopping immediately on the first mismatch, then
reporting a reconstructed console transcript plus the expected/actual diff.

commitResults.messageTitle: Support package-scoped source layout in UI test
Saves the task list to file on disk
Load list from file on disk
Level-8 Minimal, dateline dates stored as java.time.LocalDate
Print Deadlines/Events using year, month or dates
Add time for Deadlines and Events, prompting time to print list of task is ignored
Extract Ui class to own all console input and output
Extract Parser class to own all command interpretation
Extract TaskList to own the task collection and its indexing
Make Storage an instance and give FF15 a constructor and run()
Replace the command switch with a Command class hierarchy
Change farewell wording to "Okie bye bye"
Organize classes into ff15.task and ff15.command packages
Point Gradle build at ff15.FF15 and name the jar ff15.jar
Add JUnit test suite covering the high-value methods
Adopt SE-EDU Git conventions in AGENTS.md
Add Javadoc to all non-private classes and methods
Comply with the SE-EDU Java coding standard
Add a find command to search task descriptions
Add Checkstyle to the Gradle build
Fix Checkstyle violations in existing code
Align coding standard skill with the Checkstyle config
Add a JavaFX Hello World window
Handle user input and reply as FF15
Skip the JavaFX classes when running the UI test plan
Close the GUI window when the user says bye
Use varargs for multi-line replies and adding tasks
End every @param description with a full stop
Assert the invariants the code relies on
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods depend on conditions established elsewhere: the parse
helpers slice input on the assumption that the command word is already
matched, the task list converts a 1-based number after checkNumber has
vetted it, and DateRange reads its two ends in order. Nothing states
those assumptions, so breaking one produces a wrong answer rather than
a failure -- a reversed date range simply matches no tasks.

Add assertions recording eight such assumptions, each at the point it
must hold. Assertions suit these because they describe what is true
when the code is correct. User mistakes stay with FF15Exception, which
is reported and recoverable. Two of the eight cover the empty-varargs
call that showMessage and add now silently accept.

Assertions are disabled unless asked for, so pass -ea to the run task.
Gradle already enables them when running the tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the dead standardInput setting from the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The run task pipes System.in into the application, from when gradlew
run started the console session. The entry point is now the JavaFX
launcher, which never reads standard input, so the setting changes
nothing about what the build produces.

Delete it. Configuration that does nothing still costs a reader the
effort of working out what it is for, and the console main can still
be run directly with java -cp when it is wanted.

Javadoc @param descriptions all end with a full stop, but the @throws
descriptions sitting beside them in the same comment do not. A single
block therefore mixes both styles, which reads as an oversight rather
than a decision.

The coding standard names only parameter descriptions, so neither form
breaks it. Consistency inside one comment is worth more than the
narrow reading, and both @return tags were already punctuated by hand,
which suggests the wider rule was always the intent.

Punctuate the 16 remaining @throws descriptions. Parser's spans two
lines, so its full stop goes at the end of the continuation rather
than after the first line.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the argument markers used when parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
parseDeadline and parseEvent each write their marker twice: once to
find it with indexOf, and again to skip past it with length(). Six
literals stand in for three markers, and changing one without its
partner slices the description at the wrong offset -- a wrong answer
rather than an error.

Pull the three markers out as constants, so each is written once and
the substring arithmetic reads against a name. The literals were also
the only record of the /by, /from and /to syntax, which is worth
stating plainly for anyone adding a command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Simplify the guard on a malformed event command
commitResults.messageBody:
The guard in parseEvent tests three conditions in one expression, and
the last of them, toIndex < fromIndex, requires the reader to work out
that it means the user typed /to before /from.

Name each condition. The guard then reads as the three ways an event
command can be malformed, which is what the message it throws already
says in words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the field counts of the save format
commitResults.messageBody:
parseTask calls requireFieldCount with a bare 3, 4 or 5, each followed
by a comment saying which fields the number covers. The numbers carry
no meaning on their own, and the comments have to be kept in step with
the format by hand.

Replace them with named constants and drop the comments they made
redundant. The name now says what the number counts, at the one place
the save format is defined.

Task exposes description and isDone as protected, so any subclass may
read or write them directly. No subclass does: Todo, Deadline and
Event pass the description to the constructor and reach the rest
through toString and toFileFormat.

Narrow both to private, and make description final since nothing
reassigns it. Widening access later is easy; discovering which of
three subclasses quietly writes to a field is not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams where a loop only filters or maps
commitResults.messageBody:
Four loops exist only to filter or transform a collection: the two
searches in TaskList, the save-format conversion in Storage, and the
command-word lookup in CommandWord. Each spends most of its lines on
the mechanics of accumulating a result rather than on the condition
that decides what goes in it.

Rewrite them as streams, so each reads as the one operation it
performs. CommandWord.match gains a small matches() helper: the
condition it tests needs four lines of explanation, which belongs in a
named method rather than inside a lambda.

The two TaskList searches collect into an ArrayList rather than using
toList(), because callers are handed a copy they may modify, and two
tests rely on that by clearing the result. Storage.load is left as a
loop: parseTask throws a checked exception, which map() cannot carry.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a contact model and list
commitResults.messageBody:
A contact is not a task: it has no done state, no dates, and nothing to
mark. Extending Task would give every contact behaviour that makes no
sense for it, and would put contacts in the middle of the task list.

Add a separate package holding a Contact and the list that owns them.
The list mirrors TaskList deliberately -- the same 1-based numbering,
the same guard against numbers nobody has, the same assertions -- so
anyone who knows one knows the other.

Only the name is required. A phone or an email left out is stored empty
and never shown back to the user, so a contact with just a name shows as
just that name rather than as a row of blanks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Carry a contact list through the program
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing outside the new package can reach a contact: Storage owns one
file and one format, Command.execute takes only a TaskList, and the Ui
knows how to show tasks alone.

Give Storage a second path, widen execute by one parameter, and build
the contact list beside the task list at startup. Each command uses
whichever list it works on and ignores the other, which keeps one
execute for all of them rather than a second hierarchy dispatched on by
type. These three changes are one change in practice, since none of them
compiles without the others.

Contacts live in their own file so the task format is untouched and a
save file written before contacts existed still loads. A saved contact
always writes all three fields, so a name-only one ends in two empty
fields -- which is why the split passes -1 as its limit, the default
having dropped them and lost the name. The two files are read in
separate try blocks, so a damaged one does not cost the user the other.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the contact commands and their parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
The contact list is reachable from a command but nothing builds one, so
there is still no way for the user to record anyone.

Add add, list, delete and find behind a single 'contact' word rather
than four top-level verbs, so the feature groups under one word and adds
no more as it grows. Task find is left alone: it searches descriptions
only, and contact find searches names only, so neither surprises the
user with the other's results.

The /phone and /email markers may come in either order and either may be
left out. Both are checked lightly -- a phone's characters, and an email
having one @ with text on both sides -- which catches an obvious mistake
without refusing an unusual but legitimate value. Markers carry a
leading space so a name may contain one, and the line is padded before
searching so that "contact add /phone 123" is a missing name rather than
a contact named after the marker.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover contacts in the UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
The plan drove every command the chatbot had, so the console runner
exercised the whole command set. Contacts were not in it.

Add cases for each sub-command, for the input each one rejects, and for
two things worth pinning down: find does not match a contact, and list
does not show one. The plan still ends with everything deleted, so both
save files are left empty for the next run.
